chunks: Phone vibration motors (ERM and LRA). The question: What sort of motors are typically used for phone's vibration motor?
Phone buzzers come in two kinds. An ERM is a tiny motor with a lopsided weight, so it shakes as it spins.
An LRA is a coil that pushes a small weight back and forth on a spring, like a tiny speaker. LRAs give sharper, more controllable buzzes and are common in modern phones.
An ERM is like a washing machine with all the laundry bunched on one side: the unbalanced spin shakes everything.
An LRA is like pushing a child on a swing at just the right rhythm: small pushes at the right pace make a big swing. The swing example also shows the catch.
Push at the wrong rhythm and little happens, so the LRA must be driven at its resonant frequency.
Force grows with the square of speed, so doubling voltage (and so speed) gives about four times the force and doubles the vibration frequency.
You cannot have "strong but low-frequency" buzz from an ERM.
ERM: eccentric rotating mass, a small motor with an off-center weight. LRA: linear resonant actuator, a coil driving a mass on a spring.
Resonance: the natural rhythm at which a mass on a spring moves most easily. Frequency (Hz): how many shakes happen per second. 100 hertz means 100 per second.
Haptics: using vibration to give touch feedback.
An ERM spinning at 6,000 rpm (revolutions per minute) turns 6,000 / 60 = 100 times a second, so it shakes at 100 hertz.
Spin it faster and it buzzes harder and higher, since strength and frequency are tied together.
An LRA driven at its resonance of, say, 200 hertz moves back and forth every 1/200 = 5 milliseconds. It starts and stops in a few milliseconds, so you get a crisp tap.
That is the whole idea: ERM is simple and a bit mushy, LRA is sharp and programmable.

LRAs are voice-coil actuators: a mass on a spring driven by an AC signal at its resonance, around 150 to 250 hertz.
They respond in milliseconds, so they give crisp, programmable haptics, and amplitude is independent of frequency. Most modern phones use LRAs with a haptic driver IC."
